questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: `Base` is final and cannot be inherited from
It compiles, because classes are open by default
It compiles with a warning suggesting `open`
It compiles but fails at runtime with `VerifyError` when `Child` is loaded
questions.explanation: Kotlin classes are `final` by default, unlike Java. You have to mark `Base` as `open` (or `abstract`) before anything can extend it, and the compiler rejects this outright rather than warning.

questions.question: This code compiles, because a member marked `override` is itself open unless it is also marked `final`.
questions.explanation: An `override` member stays open, so `C` can override `B.f()` again without `B` writing `open`. To stop further overriding, `B` would have to declare `final override fun f()`. The class `B` itself still has to be `open`.

questions.question: You want a shared `BaseFragment` that stores `private var _binding: ViewBinding?` and nulls it in `onDestroyView()` for every screen. Why does this have to be an abstract class and not an interface?
options: Interfaces can't hold state: `_binding` has no backing field to live in
Interfaces can't contain function bodies, so `onDestroyView()` couldn't null it
Interfaces can't declare properties at all, only abstract functions
Interface methods can't be overridden by a `Fragment`
questions.explanation: Interfaces can declare properties and give methods default bodies, but they have no backing fields, so they can't store `_binding`. Abstract classes can hold state, have constructors, and extend another class like `Fragment`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `super<Focusable>.show()` calls that interface's default body, and `super<Clickable>.show()` calls the other one. They are concatenated in the order written. The order of the interfaces in the class header doesn't matter.

questions.question: Both interfaces provide a default `hi()`. What happens?
options: Compile error: `C` must override `hi`, since it inherits two implementations
Prints A, because the first interface in the supertype list always takes priority
Prints B, because the last interface wins
Throws `IllegalStateException` at runtime because the call is ambiguous
questions.explanation: Kotlin never picks one default for you based on declaration order. When a class inherits several implementations of the same member, it must override it, and can then delegate with `super<A>.hi()` or `super<B>.hi()`.

questions.explanation: A `fun interface` has exactly one abstract method, so a lambda can implement it through SAM conversion. `"  "` contains only whitespace, so `isNotBlank()` is false for it and true for `"ok"`.

questions.question: Which of these can a Kotlin interface declare? Select all that apply.
options: An abstract property like `val id: String`
A property with a custom getter like `val tag: String get() = "Repo"`
A function with a default implementation
A property with an initializer like `val retries: Int = 3`
questions.explanation: Interfaces can have abstract properties, properties computed by a getter, and default method bodies. They have no backing fields, so property initializers are not allowed, and they have no constructors. Use an abstract class when you need either.

questions.question: This is the BaseActivity-style template method pattern in plain Kotlin. What does it print?
options:
setup > home > done
setup > profile > done
questions.explanation: The final `start()` fixes the order: setup, then the subclass's `render()`, then the `onStarted` hook. `Home` keeps the default hook, which adds "done". `Profile` overrides it with an empty body, so nothing is added and no implicit `super` call happens.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: property initializers are not allowed in interfaces
It compiles, and every implementer inherits "unknown" as the default value
It compiles, but `name` must still be overridden
It compiles only if `name` is changed to `var`
questions.explanation: An initializer needs a backing field, and interfaces can't have one. To give a default you write a getter instead: `val name: String get() = "unknown"`.

questions.question: This compiles.
questions.explanation: A `var` promises a setter, and a `val` override would take that setter away, so overriding `var` with `val` is rejected. The reverse is allowed: a `val` only promises a getter, so a `var` override just adds a setter.

questions.question: `BaseActivity` declares `protected fun showLoading()`. In Kotlin, where can `showLoading()` be called from?
options: Inside `BaseActivity`, its subclasses, and any class in the same package
Anywhere in the same Gradle module
questions.explanation: Kotlin's `protected` means the declaring class plus its subclasses. Unlike Java, Kotlin has no package-level visibility, so a helper class in the same package can't call it.

questions.question: In a multi-module Android project, `:core:data` declares `internal class UserMapper`. The `:app` module depends on `:core:data`. What happens when a class in `:app` uses `UserMapper`?
options: Compile error: `internal` is visible only inside its own module
It works if the class in `:app` is in the same package as `UserMapper`
It compiles but crashes at runtime with `IllegalAccessError`
questions.explanation: `internal` means visible within one module, which in Android is a Gradle module compiled together. A dependency doesn't open it up, and package names don't matter. This is how a module keeps implementation details hidden behind its public API.

questions.question: What happens when you compile this?
options: Compile error: `f` in `B` is final and cannot be overridden
Compile error: `final` and `override` modifiers can't be combined on one member
questions.explanation: `final override` overrides `A.f()` and closes it for further subclasses. `B` being `open` only lets you extend the class, not override its final members, and `A.f()` being open doesn't matter once `B` has sealed it.

questions.question: This fake for unit tests compiles, because its `getUser` signature matches the interface.
questions.explanation: Kotlin requires the explicit `override` modifier. A matching signature isn't enough, so this is an error: the member hides the inherited one, and the class also doesn't implement the abstract `getUser`. Write `override suspend fun getUser(...)`.

questions.question: What does this print?
questions.explanation: `super.greet()` runs `A`'s body, but inside it `name()` is still a virtual call on the same `B` object, so it resolves to `B.name()`. `super` only changes which `greet` body runs, not how calls inside it dispatch.

questions.question: Which function fails to compile?
questions.explanation: From inside `Derived`, a protected member can be accessed only through a receiver of type `Derived` (or a subtype). Through a plain `Base` reference it's rejected, because that object might be a different subclass entirely. Accessing `other.secret` on another `Derived` is fine.

questions.question: Which statements about Kotlin visibility are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A `private` top-level function is visible only inside the file that declares it
A declaration with no visibility modifier is `public`
`internal` means visible inside the same package
An outer class can access `private` members of its nested class
A `private constructor` can still be called from the class's own companion object
questions.explanation: Top-level `private` is file-scoped, the default is `public`, and the companion object counts as inside the class, so it can call a private constructor. `internal` is about modules, not packages. Unlike Java, a Kotlin outer class can't see `private` members of a nested class.
